title: Marine forms of life change almost simultaneously throughout the world

fields.label: Label
fields.value: Marine forms of life change almost simultaneously throughout the world

fields.label: Statement
fields.value: The forms of marine life change almost simultaneously, in a broad geological sense, throughout the world, so that formations in distant regions under different climates can be correlated by their fossils.

fields.label: Work
fields.value: On the Origin of Species by Means of Natural Selection, or the Preservation of Favoured Races in the Struggle for Life

fields.label: Chapter
fields.value: Ch. X: On the Geological Succession of Organic Beings

fields.label: Quotation
fields.value: Scarcely any palæontological discovery is more striking than the fact, that the forms of life change almost simultaneously throughout the world.

fields.label: Agent
fields.value: delphisci Origin of Species claim extractor

fields.label: Assumptions
fields.value: Charles Darwin, On the Origin of Species (1st ed., London: John Murray, 1859), Chapter X, “On the Geological Succession of Organic Beings”; section “On simultaneous changes in the forms of life throughout the world”. Scope: marine faunas across continents and climates

fields.label: Assessment
fields.value: GPT-5.6 Sol on darwin1859-ch10-12: resolvable-now, resolvability 0.86

fields.label: Finding
fields.value: Marine biostratigraphy and global occurrence data directly target the proposition. Independent radiometric constraints can limit circularity, leaving a highly feasible and discriminating analysis.

fields.label: Proposed test in the assessment
fields.value: Proposed test with existing data: Compare dated marine assemblage turnover horizons among regions and climates using shared taxa and compositional change. Estimate global synchronicity relative to dating uncertainty and test whether fossil-based correlations outperform geography or climate alone.

fields.label: Evidence against
fields.value:
Biochronological dating can be circular when fossils also define ages.

'Almost simultaneously' is scale-dependent.

fields.label: Finding
fields.value: Cross-regional marine turnover is densely recorded, and independent age frameworks exist so the test need not use the fossils as their own clock. Agreement within a stage is a concrete criterion matching the broad geological sense of the claim. Coverage is stronger for shelly and microfossil faunas than for every marine group.

fields.label: Proposed test in the assessment
fields.value: Proposed test with existing data: Date marine faunal turnovers with radiometric, paleomagnetic, or chemostratigraphic ages and compare their timing across paleocontinents. Turnover coincident within a geological stage worldwide would support the claim; multi-stage diachrony as the usual pattern would refute it.

fields.label: Evidence against
fields.value:
Correlation that uses the fossils themselves makes simultaneity circular.

Independent dates are dense in some periods and sparse in others.

fields.label: Hypothesis
fields.value: Marine faunas on different continents change in step: the genus composition of a stage on one continent identifies the same (or an adjacent) stage on the other continents, and the magnitude of faunal change between consecutive stages is correlated across continents.

fields.label: Method
fields.value: PBDB data service 1.2: ICS stage list (intervals/list.json?scale=1, type 'age'; 95 stages with duration >= 1 Myr) and, for each stage and each of six PBDB continents (cc=NOA, SOA, EUR, AFR, ASI, AUS), the marine Metazoa genus list from occs/taxa.json (rank=genus, envtype=marine, timerule=major): 570 API calls, cached and hashed individually (derived/files.json). (A) For every continent-stage with >= 100 genera (357 of them), the Jaccard similarity of its genus list with the pooled genus list of the other five continents was computed for all 95 stages and the best-matching stage recorded (derived/stage_matching.csv). (B) For every continent, proportional genus loss between consecutive stages (1 - |G_i & G_i+1| / |G_i|, both stages >= 100 genera) was computed; Spearman correlation of these series between every continent pair with >= 10 shared boundaries (13 pairs), and a permutation test of the mean pairwise rho (stage order permuted independently within each continent, 2000 permutations, seed fixed in analysis.py). Verdict follows the pre-registered rule: supported requires (A) >= 85% same-or-adjacent and (B) mean rho > 0 with p < 0.01; refuted if (A) < 60% or (B) mean rho <= 0; otherwise mixed.

fields.label: Pass criterion
fields.value: Pre-registered. Using Paleobiology Database marine Metazoa genus lists per ICS stage (stages >= 1 Myr) for each of six PBDB continents (North America, South America, Europe, Africa, Asia, Australia), (A) for every continent-stage with >= 100 genera, find the stage whose pooled genus list from the other five continents has the highest Jaccard similarity with it; and (B) for every continent, compute the series of proportional genus loss between consecutive stages (fraction of genera in stage i absent from stage i+1, both stages >= 100 genera) and the Spearman correlation of this series between every pair of continents. The claim is SUPPORTED if in (A) the best-matching stage is the same or an adjacent stage for >= 85% of continent-stages, AND in (B) the mean pairwise Spearman correlation is > 0 with permutation p < 0.01 (independent permutation of stage order within each continent, 2000 permutations).

fields.label: Fail criterion
fields.value: Pre-registered. The claim is REFUTED if the same-or-adjacent matching rate in (A) is < 60%, or the mean pairwise correlation in (B) is <= 0. Other outcomes are 'mixed'. Exact-stage matching rate, matching rate within two stages, and per-continent-pair correlations are reported as supplementary numbers.

fields.label: Unit
fields.value: fraction of continent-stages (>= 100 genera) whose fauna best matches the same or an adjacent stage on the other continents

fields.label: Interpretation
fields.value: Darwin's 'forms of life change almost simultaneously throughout the world' is operationalised by its own consequence, which he states: that formations in distant regions can be correlated by their fossils. Test (A) is that correlation exercise done with genera: a continent's fauna from one stage should pick out the same stage elsewhere in the world. Test (B) checks that the amount of change between consecutive stages co-varies across continents (synchronous turnover). 'Almost simultaneously, in a broad geological sense' is read as within one stage (typically 2-10 Myr). PBDB continents are the geographic units; marine environments only. Known limitation stated up front: PBDB stage assignments rest partly on biostratigraphic correlation, which makes some agreement across continents expected by construction; a failure of test (A) would nevertheless be possible if faunas were strongly provincial, and test (B) uses magnitudes of change that are not used in dating.

fields.label: Datasets
fields.value: Paleobiology Database, data service 1.2: occs/taxa (marine Metazoa genera per stage and continent) and intervals/list (stage ages)

fields.label: Caveats
fields.value:
Test (A) fell short of the pre-registered 85% bar: 78.4% (95% Wilson CI 73.9-82.4%) of continent-stages are best matched by the same or an adjacent stage elsewhere (53.8% exact, 87.4% within two stages, median offset 0). Test (B) passed clearly: mean pairwise Spearman rho of proportional genus loss = 0.31, permutation p = 0.0005; 12 of 13 continent pairs positive. The pre-registered rule therefore gives 'mixed'.

Matching success depends strongly on sampling: Europe 88%, Asia 86%, North America 85% (the three continents with median > 300 genera per stage) versus Africa 66%, Australia 55%, South America 54% (median 165-185 genera per stage). The failures are mostly a sampling-depth problem rather than faunal provinciality: for the 77 mismatched continent-stages the true stage's Jaccard is on average 79% of the best stage's, i.e. the correct stage is nearly tied.

Mismatches concentrate in the Neogene-Quaternary (e.g. Calabrian faunas of three continents best match the Aquitanian) where genus-level turnover is low and many genera persist for the whole period, and in thin Permian/Oligocene records. Low turnover is the opposite of what would falsify Darwin's claim (asynchronous change), so the 'mixed' verdict understates support for synchrony of change while correctly recording that genus lists alone cannot date stages to within one stage on poorly sampled continents.

PBDB stage assignments of collections rest partly on biostratigraphic correlation, so some cross-continent agreement in (A) is expected by construction; test (B) uses magnitudes of turnover, which are not used in dating, and is the more independent test. The PBDB is a live database; the retrieved responses are hashed and dated so the run can be audited but later runs may differ.

Darwin's claim is about marine forms changing 'almost simultaneously throughout the world'; it is here reduced to genus composition of marine Metazoa on six continental units at stage resolution (typically 2-10 Myr). It does not test synchrony at finer than stage resolution.
